name: Images, compression and ZIP archives
title: Image formats, metadata, compression and ZIP files, explained simply
metaTitle: Convert Images, Remove Metadata, Compress and Zip Files
metaDescription: Convert image formats, create a metadata-free copy, compress photos, or make and open ZIP files. Everything runs locally in your browser.
intro: Not every file job is a PDF job. Sometimes a form wants a JPG and you have a PNG. Sometimes a website refuses a 9 MB photograph and wants it under 2 MB. Sometimes you want to share pixels without camera details or an embedded provenance record. Sometimes you need to send eleven files to someone who can only accept one attachment. These guides cover the everyday file work that surrounds documents: changing an image format, making a metadata-free copy, making a picture smaller without it looking chewed, and packing or unpacking a ZIP archive. These tools run inside your browser tab, so the files never leave your computer and no monthly quota applies to any of them.
answer: Use an image converter to change a picture between JPG, PNG and WebP, an image metadata remover to make a clean copy without common embedded records, an image compressor to cut its file size, and a ZIP tool to pack or unpack files. Everything runs in your browser, so nothing is uploaded.
primaryKeyword: convert and compress images and zip files

posts.title: How to convert an image between JPG, PNG, WebP and AVIF
posts.metaTitle: How to Convert an Image: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF
posts.metaDescription: JPG, PNG, WebP or AVIF: what each format is good at, how to convert between them in your browser, and why converting JPG to PNG never restores lost detail.
posts.answer: Open the image in a converter, pick the format you want, and download the result. Photographs belong in JPG or WebP; screenshots, logos, diagrams and anything needing transparency belong in PNG. Converting is one-way for quality: turning a JPG into a PNG cannot bring back detail the JPG already threw away.

body.x: An image file is two things: a grid of coloured dots, and a set of rules for writing that grid down without using an absurd amount of space. The format is the rulebook. Converting means unpacking the picture with one rulebook and repacking it with another. That is why some conversions cost you nothing and others quietly cost you detail you can never get back.
The four formats you will actually meet

body.caption: The same photograph and the same screenshot, saved four ways.
head: Format
Compression
Transparency
Use it for
rows: Lossy: it discards detail to save space, and you choose how much
Photographs, and anything else made of soft gradients rather than hard edges
Lossless: every pixel comes back exactly as it went in
Screenshots, logos, diagrams, line art, and anything that needs a see-through background
Web images generally. Roughly 25 to 35 percent smaller than JPG at the same visual quality
The smallest of the four at a given quality, often around half the size of the equivalent JPG

body.x: The one rule that covers most decisions: **photographs go to JPG or WebP, anything with flat colour, sharp text or transparency goes to PNG.** A holiday photo saved as PNG is typically five to ten times larger than the JPG for no visible gain. A screenshot of a spreadsheet saved as JPG comes back with faint smeared halos around every letter and number, because JPG was designed for skin tones and skies, not for a hard black line meeting a white background.
Converting, step by step

items.x: For an iPhone photo, open the [HEIC to JPG converter](/tools/heic-to-jpg). For other formats, use the [image converter](/tools/image-converter) and drop the picture in. The file is decoded in the tab you are looking at. Nothing is uploaded, no account is needed, and there is no monthly allowance to run down.

Choose the target from the list. If a website or a form told you what it accepts, use exactly that. Forms that say "JPG only" usually mean it, and renaming a `.png` file to `.jpg` does not convert anything: the contents are still PNG and the upload will be rejected.

items.h: Set the quality, if the target is lossy
items.x: JPG, WebP and AVIF all take a quality number. 80 is a sensible default for photographs. PNG has no quality setting, because it never throws anything away.

items.h: Check the size before you commit
items.x: The output size is shown next to the preview. If a 4 MB photograph converts to a 30 KB JPG, the quality is set far too low; if it converts to 6 MB, you have probably picked PNG by mistake.
The converted file downloads with the new extension. Rename it now if it is going somewhere fussy, because `IMG_4471 (2).jpg` is not a filename anybody wants attached to an insurance claim.

body.x: Convert between JPG, PNG, WebP and AVIF in your browser. The picture never leaves your computer.
Converting a JPG to PNG does not improve it

This is the single thing most people get wrong. PNG is lossless, so the conversion is faithful, but it is faithful **to the JPG**, blur and blocks and all. The detail JPG discarded when the photo was first saved is gone from the file. PNG has nothing to reconstruct it from, so all you get is a much larger file containing exactly the same damage.

The same logic applies to quality numbers. Re-saving a quality 60 JPG at quality 95 does not restore anything either. It just stores the already-degraded picture more carefully. If you need a better version, you need the original: the camera file, the design file, or the person who sent it. There is no software anywhere that recovers detail a lossy format has already thrown away, however confidently it claims otherwise.

Converting the other way, PNG to JPG, is a real loss and happens the moment you press convert. Keep the PNG. If the JPG turns out to be too soft or the wrong size, you want the untouched original to try again from.
Transparency, and what JPG does to it

PNG, WebP and AVIF can store a transparent background: a logo with nothing behind it, a signature with no white box around it, an icon that sits on any colour. JPG cannot. It has no way to record "nothing here", so a converter has to fill those pixels with something, normally white or black.

That is how a transparent logo ends up as a white rectangle on a dark website header. If your image has transparency you care about, your options are PNG, WebP or AVIF, and there is no clever setting that makes JPG behave. If you are pulling a transparent graphic out of a document, [PDF to PNG with transparency](/blog/images/pdf-to-png-transparent) covers that route.
HEIC, the format your iPhone hands you

Photographs taken on a recent iPhone are saved as HEIC by default, which is about half the size of JPG at the same quality but is refused by a great many websites, printers and older Windows machines. Converting HEIC to JPG is the fix, and it is the most common image conversion people ever do.

items: **Stop it happening again**: on the iPhone, Settings, Camera, Formats, choose **Most Compatible**. New photos are then JPG. Existing ones stay HEIC.
**Convert what you already have**: run the file through a converter and choose JPG. Quality 85 keeps the difference invisible.
**Emailing or AirDropping first**: sending a HEIC photo to a Windows PC via most mail apps converts it to JPG on the way, which is sometimes all you need.

body.x: Which format if it is going on paper

Print does not care about WebP or AVIF, and many print shops will not accept either. For anything printed, use JPG at high quality or PNG, and worry about the pixel dimensions rather than the format: an image needs roughly 300 dots per inch at its printed size, so a photo filling a 6 by 4 inch print wants around 1800 by 1200 pixels. [Choosing an image format for print](/blog/images/best-image-format-for-print) works through the arithmetic properly.

Once the format is right, the next question is usually size. If the file is still too heavy for an upload limit, [compressing the image](/blog/files/compress-an-image) is the next step, and if you are collecting several pictures to send as one document, [turn them into a PDF](/tools/jpg-to-pdf) instead of attaching eleven separate files.

faqs.q: Does converting a JPG to PNG improve the quality?
faqs.a: No. PNG stores the JPG faithfully, including every bit of blur and blocking the JPG already had. The detail JPG discarded is not in the file any more, so nothing can bring it back. You just get a much bigger file with the same flaws.

faqs.q: Should I use JPG or PNG?
faqs.a: Photographs to JPG, everything with flat colour, sharp text or transparency to PNG. A screenshot saved as JPG gets smeared halos around the text; a photograph saved as PNG is five to ten times larger with no visible gain.

faqs.q: Is WebP better than JPG?
faqs.a: For anything shown on screen, usually yes. WebP is around 25 to 35 percent smaller at the same visual quality and it supports transparency, which JPG does not. For print or for a form that demands JPG, stick with JPG.

faqs.q: Can I just rename a .png file to .jpg?
faqs.a: No. The extension is only a label; the contents are still PNG. Some software will open it anyway, but strict uploads and print systems read the file itself and reject it. Convert properly instead, which takes a couple of seconds.

faqs.q: How do I convert an iPhone HEIC photo to JPG?
faqs.a: Run it through an image converter and choose JPG at quality 85. To stop it recurring, open Settings, Camera, Formats on the iPhone and pick Most Compatible so new photos are saved as JPG from the start.

posts.title: How to compress an image without it looking wrecked
posts.metaTitle: How to Compress an Image Without Losing Quality
posts.metaDescription: Make a photo smaller without it looking wrecked. What the quality slider actually does, why re-saving a JPG degrades it every time, and why resizing wins.
secondaryKeywords: make a photo smaller in mb
posts.answer: Drop the picture into a compressor, lower the quality setting until the preview starts to look soft, then step back one notch and download. Quality around 75 to 80 removes most of the file size and little of the detail. If the image is bigger than it needs to be on screen, cutting its pixel dimensions saves far more than any quality slider.

body.x: There are only two ways to make an image file smaller, and they are not equal. You can keep the same number of pixels and describe each one less precisely, which is what a quality slider does. Or you can keep fewer pixels, which is what resizing does. Most people reach for the first and ignore the second, which is backwards: resizing usually wins by a much larger margin and costs nothing visible.
What the quality number actually means

A JPG quality setting is not a percentage of anything you can see. It controls how aggressively the encoder rounds off fine variation, mostly in areas where the eye is bad at noticing. The relationship between the number and the file size is steep at the top and flat in the middle, which is why the first few notches are nearly free.

body.caption: A 4032 by 3024 phone photograph, 4.8 MB out of the camera, saved at different JPG quality settings.
head: Quality
File size
What you see
rows: Indistinguishable from 95, at nearly double the size. Never worth it
Visually identical to the original for any normal use
The sweet spot. You would need to zoom in and hunt to find a difference
Fine on screen. Slight softening in fine texture such as hair or foliage
Visible blocking in flat areas like a clear sky. Acceptable for a thumbnail
Obvious mush. Only for a placeholder you intend to replace

body.x: The lesson is the shape of that column, not the exact numbers. Going from 100 to 80 removed three quarters of the file and nothing you can see. Going from 80 to 50 removed another half and made the picture visibly worse. Stop where the curve flattens.
Resizing is the bigger win

File size scales with the number of pixels, and pixel count scales with the square of the dimensions. Halve the width and the height and you are storing a quarter of the pixels before compression even starts. That 4032 by 3024 photograph is 12.2 million pixels. A full-width image on a web page rarely needs more than 1600 pixels across, which is 1.9 million pixels, six times fewer.

body.caption: Sensible maximum dimensions by destination, for the same source photograph.
head: Where it is going
Long edge
Typical size at quality 80
rows: Full-width image on a web page
Uploaded to a form with a 2 MB cap
900 KB to 1.5 MB, and keep quality at 90

body.x: Do both, in this order: resize first, then compress. Resizing throws away pixels the destination was never going to show, and compressing what is left is much more effective than compressing the full-size version. The reverse order wastes the compression work entirely.
Compressing, step by step

items.x: Go to [compress image](/tools/compress-image) and drop the picture in. It is processed inside your browser tab, so the photo is never uploaded anywhere and there is no usage limit to worry about.
If the long edge is larger than the table above suggests, bring it down. This is the change that does the heavy lifting.

items.h: Lower the quality until it looks soft
items.x: Drag down and watch the preview at full size, not the thumbnail. When you first notice softening, go back one notch. For most photographs you will land between 75 and 85.

items.h: Check the number, not the feeling
items.x: Compare the before and after sizes. If you needed under 2 MB and you are at 1.1 MB, stop. Squeezing further is free damage.
Save the compressed copy under a new name. Never overwrite the source, because the next time someone asks for a bigger version you will want it back.

body.x: Shrink a photograph in your browser. Resize and compress in one pass, with nothing uploaded.
Why re-saving the same JPG keeps making it worse

Every time a JPG is decoded and saved again as a JPG, it is compressed again from scratch, on top of the damage from last time. This is called generation loss. Open, crop, save. Open, rotate, save. Open, adjust brightness, save. Three rounds of that on a quality 80 file and the sky has gone blotchy, even though you never touched the quality setting.

The habit that avoids it: keep one master file, make all your edits in one sitting, and export a JPG at the end. If you must edit repeatedly, work from a PNG and only convert to JPG for the final version. And never use a compressed copy as the starting point for the next job, which is the most common way a photograph ends up looking like a photocopy of a photocopy.
PNG is a different problem

PNG is lossless, so it has no quality slider to drag. It gets smaller in other ways: reducing the number of distinct colours it stores, stripping metadata, and choosing better internal filtering. A screenshot with a handful of flat colours can drop 60 or 70 percent from colour reduction alone with no visible change at all.

items: **A screenshot that is inexplicably huge** is usually a Retina or high-DPI capture at double the pixels you need. Halve the dimensions and it will look identical on a normal screen.

**A photograph saved as PNG** is not a compression problem, it is a format problem. Convert it to JPG or WebP and the file drops by 80 to 90 percent. See [converting an image format](/blog/files/convert-an-image-format).
**A logo or diagram** should stay PNG. Pushing it into JPG to save 40 KB gives you fuzzy edges around every line, which is a bad trade on a file that small.

**Metadata** rides along in both formats: camera model, lens, software, and often the GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken. Most compressors strip it, which shrinks the file slightly and removes the location, an accidental privacy win.

body.x: When the real problem is the email, not the image

If photos will not send, check the current sender and recipient limits before resizing them. Limits vary by service and account; encoding and message content can also affect delivery. If the service allows it, share a link instead of reducing an image so far that it is no longer useful.

If it is a set of pictures rather than one, two other routes beat compression. [Pack them into a ZIP](/blog/files/how-to-make-a-zip-file) so they arrive as a single attachment, or [combine them into one PDF](/tools/jpg-to-pdf) if the recipient is going to look through them in order. For document attachments that are too big, [reducing a PDF for email](/blog/compress/reduce-pdf-file-size-for-email) is the equivalent guide.

faqs.q: What quality setting should I use for JPG?
faqs.a: Around 80 for most photographs. Going from 100 to 80 typically removes three quarters of the file size with nothing visible lost. Below about 60 you start seeing blocky patches in flat areas such as skies.

faqs.q: Does compressing an image lose quality?
faqs.a: JPG and lossy WebP do lose a little, permanently. PNG compression does not lose anything. The trick is to stop at the point where the file is small enough but the loss is still invisible, which for photographs is usually quality 75 to 85.

faqs.q: Why does my image get worse every time I save it?
faqs.a: Each save re-compresses the picture on top of the previous compression. That is generation loss. Edit once from a master file and export a single final JPG, rather than opening and re-saving the same JPG repeatedly.

faqs.q: Is it better to resize or to compress?
faqs.a: Resize first, then compress. Halving the width and height stores a quarter of the pixels, which beats any quality slider, and compressing the smaller version afterwards is far more effective than compressing the full-size one.

faqs.q: How do I get a photo under 2 MB?
faqs.a: Set the long edge to about 2000 pixels and the quality to 80. A typical phone photograph lands well under 500 KB that way, with no visible difference on any screen.

posts.title: How to make a ZIP file, and when zipping is pointless
posts.metaTitle: How to Make a ZIP File (and When Not To)
posts.metaDescription: A ZIP is one folder-shaped file holding many. Learn how to make one, when zipping actually shrinks things, and when it saves you nothing at all.
posts.primaryKeyword: how to make a zip file
secondaryKeywords: send many files as one attachment
posts.answer: Select the files, add them to a ZIP tool, and download the single .zip that comes out. A ZIP is one file that holds many, and it compresses them on the way in. Documents, spreadsheets and text shrink a lot. JPGs, MP4s and PDFs are already compressed, so zipping them mainly makes them convenient, not smaller.

body.x: A ZIP file does two jobs at once, and confusing them is why people are disappointed by it. First, it is a container: many files and folders wrapped into one file, with a small index at the end recording what is inside and where each piece starts. Second, it compresses each of those files as it packs them. The container part always works. The compression part depends entirely on what you put in.
What actually shrinks, and what does not

Compression works by finding repetition. A text file that says the same words over and over compresses beautifully. A file that has already been compressed has had its repetition removed, so there is nothing left to find. Squeezing it again gains you almost nothing, and occasionally the archive is a few kilobytes larger than the original because of the bookkeeping.

body.caption: Typical results from zipping 100 MB of each kind of file.
head: What you zip
Comes out at roughly
Why
rows: Enormously repetitive. The best case there is
Modern .docx and .xlsx are already zipped internally. Older .doc and .xls shrink much more
Large flat areas of the same colour compress well
Images and streams inside a PDF are already compressed
Nothing to win. Zip these only to bundle them together

body.x: So the honest summary: if you are zipping a folder of holiday photos hoping it will fit under an email limit, it will not. Zipping is still the right move, because it turns 40 attachments into 1, but you need to [compress the images themselves](/blog/files/compress-an-image) if size is the actual problem.
Making a ZIP, step by step

items.x: Put everything in one folder and give it the name you want the recipient to see, such as `Invoices-2026-Q1`. The folder name becomes the archive name and the folder people unpack it into, so it is worth thirty seconds of thought.

Go to [create ZIP](/tools/create-zip) and drop the files or the whole folder in. Everything is packed inside your browser tab. No file is uploaded, no account is required, and no quota is consumed however many archives you build.
Confirm the file count and the total size before packing. This is the moment to notice that you dragged in a `.DS_Store`, a duplicate, or last year's version by mistake.
The tool reports the size before and after. If the two are nearly identical, that is expected for photos, video and PDFs, and it does not mean anything went wrong.
Open the finished .zip once yourself before you send it. Ten seconds of checking prevents the message that begins "this file will not open".

body.x: Pack any set of files into one ZIP archive, entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
The real reason to zip: one attachment instead of forty

Most email clients, ticketing systems, upload forms and shared drives are far happier with one file than with dozens. Zipping also preserves the folder structure, which plain attachments cannot. If your work is organised as `Project/Photos/`, `Project/Drafts/` and `Project/Final/`, a ZIP arrives with that arrangement intact; attaching 40 loose files arrives as 40 loose files and the recipient has to guess.

items: **Sending a batch of documents** to an accountant, a solicitor or a landlord, where the order and grouping matter.
**Handing over a project** with its folders, so nobody has to reconstruct the structure at the other end.
**Getting past attachment count limits**, which some corporate mail systems set as low as ten files.
**Archiving something you are finished with**, so a hundred small files become one item in your backup.
**Protecting the file names**, since some upload forms rename or lowercase files, but leave the contents of a ZIP alone.

body.x: What a ZIP does not do

A plain ZIP is not private. Anyone who has the file can list what is inside and open every item, and the file names are readable even before extraction. Zipping a folder of bank statements protects nothing at all. If a document genuinely needs protecting, [put a password on the PDF itself](/blog/privacy/password-protect-pdf) rather than trusting the wrapper around it.

It also does not deduplicate across files in any useful way, it does not repair anything, and it does not make a corrupt file readable. And it does not speed up an upload of already-compressed material: 100 MB of video takes the same time to send whether it is bare or in an archive.
Doing it without a tool

Both desktop systems can make a ZIP with no software at all. On Windows, select the files, right-click, then **Send to**, then **Compressed (zipped) folder**. On macOS, select them, right-click, then **Compress**, which produces `Archive.zip` if you selected several items, or `Name.zip` if you selected one folder. From a terminal:

# macOS or Linux: zip a folder and everything in it
zip -r invoices-2026-q1.zip invoices-2026-q1/

# Leave macOS metadata out of the archive
zip -r -X clean.zip myfolder/

# Windows PowerShell
Compress-Archive -Path .\invoices-2026-q1\* -DestinationPath invoices-2026-q1.zip

On macOS, right-click compression quietly adds a `__MACOSX` folder and `.DS_Store` files to the archive. They are harmless but they look untidy to a Windows recipient, who sees them as mystery extra items. A browser ZIP tool or the `-X` flag above leaves them out.
ZIP or a single PDF?

If the recipient is going to read your files in order, a PDF is usually better than a ZIP. They open one document and scroll, instead of extracting an archive and opening eight files one at a time. Scans, receipts and photographed paperwork are the obvious cases: [turn the images into one PDF](/tools/jpg-to-pdf) and send that. Use a ZIP when the files are genuinely separate things, when they are not all documents, or when the folder structure carries meaning. When someone sends you one, [opening a ZIP file](/blog/files/how-to-open-a-zip-file) covers the other half of the job.

faqs.q: How do I make a ZIP file?
faqs.a: Select the files, add them to a ZIP tool or right-click and choose Compress on macOS, or Send to, Compressed folder on Windows. You get one .zip file holding everything, with the folder structure preserved.

faqs.q: Does zipping make photos smaller?
faqs.a: Almost never. JPG and PNG are already compressed, so a ZIP of 100 MB of photos comes out at 95 to 100 MB. Zip them to send one attachment instead of forty, and compress the images themselves if you need the size down.

faqs.q: What kind of files shrink the most when zipped?
faqs.a: Plain text, CSV and log files, which are highly repetitive and can drop to 10 to 25 percent of their original size. Older Word and Excel formats also shrink well. Anything already compressed barely moves.

faqs.q: Is a ZIP file secure?
faqs.a: A plain ZIP is not. Anyone with the file can list and open everything inside, and the file names are visible before extraction. For genuine protection, encrypt or password-protect the document itself rather than relying on the archive.

faqs.q: Can I email a ZIP file?
faqs.a: Usually yes, though some corporate mail filters block or quarantine ZIP attachments because malware has been distributed that way. If your archive bounces, put it in a shared drive and send the link instead.

posts.title: How to open a ZIP file on any device
posts.metaTitle: How to Open a ZIP File on Any Device
posts.metaDescription: Open a ZIP file on Windows, macOS, iPhone or Android, and see what to do when the archive is password-protected, corrupted, or not really a ZIP at all.
posts.primaryKeyword: how to open a zip file
posts.answer: On Windows, right-click the file and choose Extract All. On macOS, double-click it. On iPhone and Android, tap it in the Files app and the system unpacks it. A browser tool works on any of them and lists the contents before you extract. A password-protected ZIP needs its password; no tool can open it without one.

body.x: Opening a ZIP is called extracting or unzipping, and it means copying the files back out of the container into a normal folder. Every current phone and computer can do it without installing anything. The confusion is almost always about where the files went afterwards, or about an archive that refuses to cooperate.
The four platforms
Windows 10 and 11

items: Right-click the .zip file and choose **Extract All**.
Windows suggests a folder next to the archive with the same name. Accept it or pick another.
Tick **Show extracted files when complete** so you land in the right place, then click **Extract**.

body.x: Double-clicking a ZIP in Windows opens a preview that looks exactly like a normal folder, and this is where most people go wrong. You can browse it, but the files are still inside the archive. Running an installer or editing a document from that preview often fails with a strange permissions error, and any edits you save are thrown away. Always extract first, then work with the real files.
macOS

Double-click the archive. Archive Utility unpacks it into a folder beside it, with the same name, and there is no dialogue and no progress window for small archives. If you cannot find the result, look in the same folder as the .zip, or in **Downloads** if you opened it straight from a browser.
iPhone and iPad

Save the attachment to the **Files** app first, then tap it once. iOS unpacks it into a folder in the same location, which you can then open normally. Tapping a ZIP directly inside Mail sometimes shows a preview of the contents rather than extracting anything, so if you need the files to stick around, go through Files.
Android

Open the **Files** app, find the archive in Downloads, tap it, then tap **Extract**. You are shown a preview of the contents and where they will be saved. Some manufacturer file managers label the button **Unzip** or **Decompress** instead, but the flow is the same.
Extracting in the browser, and why you might

items.x: Go to [extract ZIP](/tools/extract-zip) and drop the archive in. It is unpacked inside your browser tab. The archive is never uploaded, nothing is stored, and there is no limit on how many you open.
You get every file name, its size and its folder, before anything is written to your disk. This is the fastest way to check whether an archive holds what you expect.
Take one file out of a hundred if that is all you want, instead of extracting the whole thing and then deleting the rest.
Selected files come out as normal files. Your original .zip is untouched, so you can go back for the rest later.

body.x: Open a ZIP and pull out just the files you want, without uploading the archive anywhere.

This route is genuinely useful in three situations: on a locked-down work computer where you cannot install archive software, on a phone whose file manager will not let you peek inside before extracting, and any time the archive is private. People zip tax returns, medical letters, contracts and family photographs, and the usual online unzipping services upload the whole archive to a server to open it. A browser tool does not, which is the entire point. [Are online file tools safe](/blog/privacy/are-online-pdf-tools-safe) sets out how to tell the difference for yourself.
Password-protected archives

If a ZIP asks for a password, you need the password. That is the whole answer. The contents are encrypted, and no tool, service or setting recovers them without the key. Anything advertising itself as a ZIP password remover is either running a slow guessing attack that only works on trivially short passwords, or it is not doing what it claims.

items: **Ask the sender.** Passwords are frequently sent in a separate message, a text, or on the covering letter of whatever the archive relates to.
**Check for a typo.** ZIP passwords are case-sensitive, and a trailing space copied along with the password is a classic failure.

**Note which kind of protection it is.** Some archives let you see the file names without the password and only encrypt the contents; others hide even the list. Seeing the names does not mean you are close to opening them.
**If you set the password and forgot it,** the files are gone unless you have another copy. This is not a case where persistence pays off.

body.x: When the archive will not open

body.caption: What the common failures mean, and what to try.
head: What you see
Usual cause
What to do
rows: Compare the file size against what the sender says it should be, then download again
Unpacks to a `.cpgz` file on macOS, endlessly
Archive Utility could not read it, often a truncated or non-ZIP file
Try the command line or a browser tool, which give a real error instead of looping
Extract the files that do work. A ZIP stores each item separately, so a bad patch does not always ruin everything
Windows says the file is in use
Wait a moment and retry, or extract it from a different folder
It is a `.rar` or `.7z`, not a `.zip`
These need their own software, such as 7-Zip on Windows or The Unarchiver on macOS

body.x: A ZIP puts its index at the end of the file, which is why a partial download so often fails outright. The first 90 percent of the data may be perfectly fine, but without the index nothing knows where anything starts. It also means a file that fails at 99 percent downloaded is no more useful than one that failed at 10 percent.
Before you extract something a stranger sent

ZIP attachments are a long-standing way of getting past mail filters, because the scanner cannot see inside as easily. Listing the contents before extracting costs nothing and tells you a lot. Treat these as reasons to stop: a `.exe`, `.scr`, `.js`, `.bat` or `.msi` file inside an archive you were not expecting; a file called something like `Invoice.pdf.exe`, where the real extension is the last one; or a single document whose name matches an email you never sent.

If the archive turns out to hold scanned pages or photographs, the next step is usually to make them into something readable. [Combine the images into one PDF](/tools/jpg-to-pdf), or if the scans are pictures of text, run them through [OCR](/blog/ocr/how-to-ocr-a-scanned-pdf) so you can search them. And if you need to send a set of files back the other way, [making a ZIP](/blog/files/how-to-make-a-zip-file) is the same job in reverse.

faqs.q: How do I open a ZIP file on Windows?
faqs.a: Right-click it and choose Extract All, then pick a destination folder. Double-clicking only previews the contents: files opened from that preview are still inside the archive, and changes you save to them are discarded.

faqs.q: How do I open a ZIP file on an iPhone?
faqs.a: Save it to the Files app, then tap it once. iOS unpacks it into a folder in the same place. Tapping the attachment directly in Mail may only show a preview without saving anything.

faqs.q: Can I open a password-protected ZIP without the password?
faqs.a: No. The contents are encrypted and there is no way around it. Ask whoever sent the archive for the password. Tools that claim to remove ZIP passwords are guessing, and that only works on very short ones.

faqs.q: Why does my ZIP turn into a .cpgz file on a Mac?
faqs.a: Archive Utility could not read the archive, usually because the download was incomplete or the file is not really a ZIP. Download it again, or open it with a tool that reports a real error rather than looping.

faqs.q: Does opening a ZIP file delete the original archive?
faqs.a: No. Extracting copies the contents out and leaves the .zip exactly where it was, so you can go back for other files later. Delete the archive yourself once you are sure you have everything.

posts.title: How to convert HEIC to JPG on iPhone, Mac and Windows
posts.metaTitle: Convert HEIC to JPG on iPhone, Mac and Windows
posts.metaDescription: Convert iPhone HEIC photos to JPG for websites, email and Windows. Learn when to convert, how to preserve the original and what quality settings mean.
posts.answer: To convert an iPhone HEIC photo to JPG, open the image in an image converter, choose JPG, check the preview and download the converted copy. Keep the original HEIC because JPG uses lossy compression. For future iPhone photos, Camera settings can switch capture to Most Compatible, which generally saves JPEG instead.

body.x: HEIC is a photo format used by many recent iPhones. It can store a good-looking image in less space than a comparable JPEG, but some upload forms, older Windows apps and print workflows do not accept it. Converting creates a broadly compatible copy; it does not repair or improve the source photo.
Convert an existing photo

items.x: Open [HEIC to JPG](/tools/heic-to-jpg), select one or more HEIC photos, and wait for the local preview to appear.
Choose JPG as the output. Use a high quality setting when the image will be printed or carefully reviewed; a smaller setting is usually adequate for a form or message.
Open the converted file and confirm that it is the right orientation and that fine details look acceptable. Keep the original until the recipient confirms the JPG works.
If a service accepts PDF but not image uploads, create a PDF from the photos with [JPG to PDF](/tools/jpg-to-pdf). If it accepts JPG, send the converted image directly.

body.x: Convert HEIC photos to JPG in your browser without sending the images to our server.
Change the format for new iPhone photos

On supported iPhones, open Settings, Camera, Formats and choose Most Compatible to prefer JPEG capture. This setting affects new photos, not the HEIC files already in your library. Menu wording can vary by iOS version. Keeping High Efficiency is reasonable when storage matters and the people or services receiving the files support HEIC.
What conversion changes

head: Question
Practical answer
rows: Does JPG work in more places?
Usually. JPEG is supported by most browsers, forms, office apps and print workflows.
Does JPG preserve every original pixel exactly?
No. JPEG is lossy. Keep the HEIC original if fidelity matters.
No. Renaming changes only the label, not the encoded image.
Yes. Metadata handling varies by converter and settings. Review location and camera metadata before sharing sensitive photos.

body.x: If a conversion fails

items: Try one photo first, especially if the original is unusually large or uses a newer HEIF variant.
Make sure the file is a still image, not a video or a motion-photo sidecar.
Download the converted output instead of changing its extension by hand.
For a sensitive image, prefer a local conversion route and inspect metadata before sharing.

body.x: HEIC-to-JPG conversion is different from [combining photos into a PDF](/blog/to-pdf/images-to-pdf): use JPG when the recipient asks for an image, and PDF when a document-style bundle is more useful.

A conversion creates another image file; it does not replace the photograph in your library unless you choose to delete the source yourself. Compare the JPG with the HEIC at the same zoom, especially around hair, foliage and small text in photographed documents. If colours look different, check whether the source uses a wide colour profile or high dynamic range and whether the target app supports it. For a photo submission, follow the receiving service instructions about maximum dimensions and file size. If it rejects the JPG, check the actual file format and size rather than repeatedly changing the extension. Keep a backup until the upload is accepted.

faqs.q: How do I change HEIC to JPG on an iPhone?
faqs.a: For an existing photo, use an image converter and choose JPG, or use an iOS share/export route that offers a compatible format. To prefer JPG for future captures, check Settings, Camera, Formats, Most Compatible. Existing HEIC files do not change automatically.

faqs.q: Will converting HEIC to JPG reduce photo quality?
faqs.a: JPEG uses lossy compression, so some image data can be discarded. Keep the original HEIC and select a high quality output when detail matters. Avoid converting the same JPG repeatedly.

faqs.q: Can I just rename a HEIC file to JPG?
faqs.a: No. The file remains HEIC internally, and software that checks the image encoding may reject it. Use a converter that decodes the HEIC image and writes a real JPEG file.

faqs.q: Is HEIC the same as HEIF?
faqs.a: HEIF is the broader image container format family. HEIC commonly refers to HEIF images that use HEVC image coding. Apps often use the terms loosely, so compatibility depends on the actual encoded file and the receiving software.

posts.title: How to remove AI metadata from an image without changing the visible picture
posts.metaTitle: Remove AI Metadata From Images Without Uploading
posts.metaDescription: Create a clean image copy without common EXIF, XMP, IPTC or C2PA metadata. Learn what is removed, what stays visible, and how to check it.
posts.answer: To remove common AI-related image metadata, create a new image file from the visible pixels rather than editing the original file in place. A fresh PNG, JPG or WebP copy drops common EXIF, IPTC, XMP and embedded C2PA or Content Credentials records, but it does not remove visible watermarks or labels.

body.x: An image can carry two kinds of information: the pixels you can see, and data attached to the file that you cannot. A camera may add its model, capture time and location. An editor may add an author name and workflow notes. Some AI image systems may add a provenance record, often called Content Credentials. They are different things, but they travel together when you send the original file.
What AI image metadata can include

body.caption: Common data stored alongside image pixels.
head: Kind of data
Examples
Visible in the picture?
rows: Camera model, date, orientation, GPS location
Author, title, keywords, editor or workflow details
An embedded provenance record about creation or edits
Watermark, caption, AI label or logo drawn into the picture

body.x: The distinction matters. File metadata can be left behind when a new file is encoded from the pixels. A visible mark is part of the pixels themselves, so a metadata tool should not claim to remove it. Altering or hiding a visible mark is a different image-editing task and can change the picture's meaning.
Remove metadata by creating a fresh copy

items.x: Save the source somewhere safe before making a sharing copy. Metadata can be useful for your own archive, even when it is not appropriate to send it on.
Go to [AI Metadata Remover](/tools/remove-ai-metadata) and add PNG, JPG, WebP or HEIC images. The file is read in your browser and is not uploaded to PrintxPDF.

Choose PNG if preserving the decoded pixels and transparency matters most. Choose JPG for ordinary photos when broad compatibility is the priority. WebP can keep transparency and is useful for web delivery.

items.h: Make and inspect the clean copy
items.x: Click Remove metadata, then download the new file. It is rebuilt from visible pixels, so common EXIF, IPTC, XMP and embedded C2PA or Content Credentials records are not copied across.

body.x: Make a metadata-free image copy locally. Your original stays untouched and your file is never uploaded.
What this does not remove

This tool does not remove watermarks, captions, logos, text prompts rendered into the picture, or an AI label you can see. Those are pixels, not metadata. It also cannot remove information a service keeps in its own account records or elsewhere outside the downloaded image file.

A new file can also change how the image is encoded. PNG is the best choice when you need exact decoded pixels. JPG and WebP use compression, so inspect a detailed area before using a sharing copy for print, evidence or production work. For a photo that needs to be smaller as well, use [Compress Image](/tools/compress-image) after you have kept a clean archival original.
When a metadata-free copy is useful

items: Sharing a phone photo without its camera model, date or possible location details.
Sending a draft image outside an editorial or design workflow without its embedded author and workflow fields.
Preparing a web image where a fresh, smaller delivery format is useful alongside a retained original.
Making a distribution copy while preserving the original file and its provenance in a controlled archive.

body.x: Removing metadata is a privacy and file-handling choice, not proof that an image was or was not made with a particular tool. Treat provenance records as one source of context, keep originals where records matter, and do not use a stripped copy to misrepresent the origin of work.

faqs.q: Does this remove ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini image metadata?
faqs.a: It removes common embedded metadata that survives browser decoding, including EXIF, IPTC, XMP and C2PA or Content Credentials records where they are stored in the image file. Providers differ, so it cannot remove a visible label or data held outside the downloaded file.

faqs.q: Will it remove an AI watermark?
faqs.a: No. A visible watermark or label is part of the pixels. This tool creates a clean file copy without common embedded metadata; it does not alter visible content.

faqs.q: Are images uploaded?
faqs.a: No. The source is decoded and the new file is encoded inside your browser. PrintxPDF does not receive the image.

faqs.q: Which output should I choose?
faqs.a: Choose PNG for transparency or exact decoded pixels, JPG for widely compatible photographs, and WebP for modern web delivery. Keep the original regardless of the format you share.

posts.title: What are Content Credentials and C2PA image metadata?
posts.metaTitle: Content Credentials and C2PA Image Metadata Explained
posts.metaDescription: Learn what C2PA and Content Credentials records are, where they live in image files, why they can disappear, and what a metadata-free copy changes.
posts.answer: Content Credentials are a type of provenance record that can be embedded in or associated with a media file using the C2PA standard. They can describe actions recorded by participating tools, but they are not a universal detector of AI-generated images and can be lost when a file is converted, resized or re-encoded.

body.x: Content Credentials are often discussed as though they are a permanent stamp inside every AI image. They are not. They are a provenance system: participating tools can record information about a media asset and attach or associate that record with the file. Whether a record exists, what it says and whether it survives sharing depends on the tool and the route the file takes.
C2PA and Content Credentials in plain language

C2PA is the technical standard behind many Content Credentials implementations. In practical terms, it gives compatible software a way to carry signed assertions about a file's history. A record might identify an application, state that edits were made, or point to a manifest associated with the asset. It is not the same as a pixel watermark, and it is not a universal verdict about whether an image is real, edited or AI-generated.

body.caption: Three concepts that are commonly mixed together.
head: Thing
Where it lives
What it can tell you
rows: What is visibly printed or drawn on the image
Camera, author, title, dates or workflow information
A provenance record embedded in or associated with the asset
Claims recorded by participating tools, when the record is present and valid

body.x: Why provenance records can disappear

Many ordinary file operations create a new image: a crop, screenshot, export, social-media upload, format conversion or compression pass. A new encoder may copy pixels but not copy every metadata block and provenance record. That does not prove anyone intended to remove the record; it only means the new file is not byte-for-byte the original. For evidence, recordkeeping or licensing work, keep the original asset and its source context rather than relying on a forwarded copy.
How a metadata-free image copy works

items.h: Separate the source from the sharing copy
items.x: Keep the original file, then make a second copy for the destination. This preserves the source for any workflow that needs its metadata or provenance.

items.h: Rebuild the copy from the visible pixels
items.x: [AI Metadata Remover](/tools/remove-ai-metadata) decodes the image in your browser and writes a new PNG, JPG or WebP. Common embedded metadata and provenance blocks are not carried into the new file.
A clean copy is appropriate for privacy or delivery requirements. It is not a basis for claiming that an image has a different origin or history than it does.

body.x: Create a local sharing copy without common embedded image metadata. Keep the original when provenance matters.
What to do when provenance matters

items: Keep the original file, rather than only a message-app or social-media copy.
Record the source, date received and relevant permissions alongside the original.
Use the software or service that supplied the record to inspect it when possible.
Do not treat the absence of a credential as proof of how an image was made.
Use a separate, clearly named delivery copy when privacy or platform requirements call for one.

body.x: Metadata removal is different from image editing. It leaves the intended visible picture alone while producing a new file. If you need a different file format or size too, see [how to convert an image format](/blog/files/convert-an-image-format) and [how to compress an image](/blog/files/compress-an-image).

faqs.q: Are Content Credentials proof that an image was made by AI?
faqs.a: No. They are provenance records from participating tools. A record may describe creation or editing actions, but its presence or absence is not a universal determination of an image's origin.

faqs.q: Can C2PA metadata be removed by converting an image?
faqs.a: A conversion or re-encoding can produce a new file without the original metadata and provenance blocks. That is why originals should be retained whenever provenance, licensing or evidence matters.

faqs.q: Does a metadata-free copy change the visible image?
faqs.a: The tool rebuilds the output from visible pixels. PNG preserves decoded pixels and transparency; JPG and WebP use compression, so check the result if fine detail is important.

faqs.q: Should I delete the original after stripping metadata?
faqs.a: Usually no. Keep the original separately, especially when it is your record of where an image came from or what its original metadata contained.
